introduction-the-hybrid-reality.core: Most enterprises run mixed fleets: Linux for web and containers, and Windows Server for Active Directory, Exchange, SQL Server, IIS-hosted .NET apps, file shares and RDS. SREs need enough Windows fluency to operate it: the object-based PowerShell, the registry instead of /etc, NTFS permissions, services and the Event Log, AD identity and Group Policy, and IIS. The concepts map to Linux equivalents, with different tools.

first_principles.problem: A Linux-focused SRE team is paged for a Windows IIS outage and doesn't know where to look.

analogy.title: Driving on the other side of the road
analogy.story: The car still has wheels, brakes and gears, but the controls are in different places.
analogy.breaks: Roads are similar; Windows' object pipeline differs fundamentally from text pipes.

check.q: What's the Windows equivalent of journalctl for reading system logs?

powershell-objects-not-text.core: PowerShell pipelines pass .NET objects with typed properties, not text. Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 100 | Sort-Object WS -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 Name,Id,WS needs no parsing with awk or cut. Commands are Verb-Noun cmdlets (Get-Service, Restart-Service), discoverable via Get-Command and Get-Help, with output inspectable via Get-Member. Remoting (Enter-PSSession, Invoke-Command) manages fleets, and PowerShell 7 runs cross-platform.

first_principles.problem: A Linux engineer tries to grep PowerShell output and breaks scripts when column widths change.

analogy.title: Passing labelled boxes vs reading a printed list
analogy.story: Each box has named compartments, so the next person picks the field they want without reading text.
analogy.breaks: Boxes are physical; objects live only inside the PowerShell pipeline until formatted.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Structured results across hosts, no parsing.

check.q: Why is parsing PowerShell output with text tools discouraged?
check.a: PowerShell passes structured objects; formatting to text loses structure and can change with display settings, making text parsing fragile.

the-registry-vs-etc.core: Windows stores much configuration in the registry, a hierarchical database of keys and values. HKLM holds machine-wide settings (services, drivers, software), HKCU per-user settings, and HKCR file associations. Values are typed (REG_SZ, REG_DWORD, REG_MULTI_SZ). Unlike /etc text files it isn't diffable in Git by default, so changes should go through PowerShell (Get-ItemProperty, Set-ItemProperty), Group Policy or DSC, with exports for backup.

first_principles.problem: A TLS hardening change made by hand in regedit on one server isn't replicated anywhere, and drifts.

analogy.title: A filing cabinet with locked drawers vs plain notebooks
analogy.story: Notebooks (/etc) are easy to photocopy and compare; the cabinet (registry) needs special tools to read and copy.
analogy.breaks: Cabinets are physical; registry hives are files loaded at boot.

code.text:
reg export 'HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\SCHANNEL' C:\backup\schannel.reg
$p = 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\SCHANNEL\Protocols\TLS 1.0\Server'
New-Item -Path $p -Force | Out-Null
Set-ItemProperty -Path $p -Name Enabled -Value 0 -Type DWord
Get-ItemProperty -Path $p

check.q: Which registry hive holds machine-wide settings like services and drivers?

ntfs-vs-linux-filesystems.core: NTFS uses rich ACLs: each file and folder has a security descriptor with an owner and ACEs granting or denying specific rights (Read, Write, Modify, Full Control and fine-grained ones) to users and groups, with inheritance from parent folders. Deny entries take precedence. Share permissions on SMB stack with NTFS permissions, and the most restrictive wins. NTFS also has alternate data streams, journaling, compression and encryption (EFS), and case-insensitive (but preserving) names.

first_principles.problem: A user has 'Full Control' on the NTFS folder but can't write over the network share.

analogy.title: Two locked doors in sequence
analogy.story: The building door (share) and the office door (NTFS) both need to let you in; the stricter lock wins.
analogy.breaks: Doors are separate; Windows computes effective access from both automatically.

code.text:
icacls D:\Shares\Finance
Get-SmbShareAccess -Name Finance
# Share: Everyone Read   ← restricts network writes despite NTFS Full Control
Grant-SmbShareAccess -Name Finance -AccountName 'CORP\Finance-Editors' -AccessRight Change -Force

check.q: How are SMB share permissions and NTFS permissions combined for network access?
check.a: Both apply, and the effective permission is the more restrictive of the two.

active-directory-ad-the-kingdom.core: Active Directory Domain Services is the central identity and policy system for Windows networks. Domain controllers hold a replicated directory of users, groups, computers and OUs; authentication uses Kerberos (with NTLM fallback); Group Policy pushes settings and security baselines to machines by OU; and DNS is tightly integrated. Compromise of AD (Domain Admins, krbtgt) means compromise of everything, which is why tiered admin models and monitoring matter.

first_principles.problem: A single helpdesk account with Domain Admin rights is phished, giving attackers control of every server.

analogy.title: A kingdom's royal registry and decrees
analogy.story: The registry says who everyone is; royal decrees (GPOs) apply to regions; whoever holds the royal seal controls the kingdom.
analogy.breaks: Kingdoms change slowly; AD compromises can spread in hours.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Visibility into who holds the keys.

code.text:
Get-ADGroupMember 'Domain Admins' -Recursive | Select-Object Name, SamAccountName
Get-ADUser alice -Properties MemberOf, LastLogonDate
gpresult /r /scope computer       # applied GPOs on this machine
Get-ADComputer -Filter * -SearchBase 'OU=Web,DC=corp,DC=example,DC=com'

check.q: Why is Domain Admin compromise so severe?
check.a: Domain Admins control AD itself, and therefore authentication and policy for every domain-joined machine and user.

managing-iis-and-rdp.core: IIS hosts web apps in sites (bindings: hostname, port, certificate) running in application pools, isolated worker processes (w3wp.exe) with their own identity, .NET runtime and recycling settings. Logs live in %SystemDrive%\inetpub\logs, and the WebAdministration and IISAdministration modules manage it. RDP gives remote desktop access. Secure it with Network Level Authentication, restricted groups, MFA and RD Gateway (never exposed directly to the internet), and use PowerShell remoting for routine work.

first_principles.problem: An IIS site returns 503 Service Unavailable because its application pool keeps crashing and was auto-stopped by rapid-fail protection.
truths: Pools can be stopped after repeated failures.
RDP is a high-value attack target.

analogy.title: A shopping mall with separate shop units
analogy.story: Each shop (app pool) has its own staff and doors; if one keeps catching fire, security closes it so the mall stays open.
analogy.breaks: Malls reopen shops manually; IIS may need you to start the pool after fixing.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Root cause found in WAS events; pool restarted.

code.text:
Import-Module WebAdministration
Get-WebAppPoolState -Name OrdersPool          # Stopped
Get-WinEvent -LogName System -MaxEvents 20 | Where-Object ProviderName -eq 'WAS' | Format-List TimeCreated, Message
# fix config/app error, then:
Start-WebAppPool -Name OrdersPool

check.q: What does an IIS 503 'Service Unavailable' commonly indicate?
check.a: The site's application pool is stopped, often by rapid-fail protection after repeated worker process crashes.
